query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The creep resistance of an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating is governed by the lattice misfit between the γ and γ′ phases, with an optimal misfit value leading to enhanced creep resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating with a γ/γ′ dual-phase microstructure
generation.intervention: Variation of the lattice misfit between the γ and γ′ phases
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice misfit between the γ and γ′ phases
generation.mechanism: The lattice misfit affects the formation and configuration of dislocation networks, which in turn influences the creep resistance of the alloy
generation.predicted_outcome: An optimal lattice misfit value will result in enhanced creep resistance, while excessive or insufficient misfit will lead to reduced creep resistance
generation.baseline: Creep resistance of the alloy with a non-optimized lattice misfit
generation.boundary: High-temperature environment with sustained stress, lattice misfit values outside the optimal range
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal lattice misfit value and the underlying mechanisms governing the creep resistance of the alloy

falsification_experiment.design: Systematic variation of the lattice misfit between the γ and γ′ phases and measurement of the resulting creep resistance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the creep resistance is not enhanced by an optimal lattice misfit value, or if the dislocation network formation is not affected by the lattice misfit, then the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: (HESAs) represent a newly developed branch of high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Owing to their γ/γ′ dual-phase microstructure and high-temperature properties comparable to those of Ni-based superalloys—combined with superior cost-effectiveness—HESAs are emerging as promising candidates for high-temperature applications. Among the key properties required for such applications, creep resistance is particularly critical, as it determines a material’s ability to withstand prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures []. Creep is a time-dependent deformation process characterized by a gradual increase in strain under stress levels below the material’s yield strength. It occurs in three distinct stages: primary, steady-state, and tertiary creep []. Primary creep, also known as transition creep, exhibits an initially high creep rate that decreases owing to the strain hardening phenomenon. This stage usually lasts for a relatively short period. Steady-state creep follows with a constant creep rate. In this process, the creation of new dislocations and annihilation of dislocations reached dynamic equilibrium, reflecting a dynamic balance between strain hardening and recovery. By adding γ′-forming elements (e.g., Ti, Al, and so on), the volume fraction of γ′ phase can be increased, thereby narrowing the γ channels, raising the critical Orowan stress required for dislocation motion within them, and enhancing the creep strength of the alloy []. For example, Mukherji et al. [] investigated the creep properties of Ni-based superalloys with different γ′ phase contents at 1100 °C/(140–210) MPa, and they demonstrated that Ni-based superalloys with up to 58% γ′ phase content exhibited longer creep lifetimes than those with 55%. However, it is worth noting that a higher volume fraction does not always lead to better performance. Indeed, it has been demonstrated that Optimal creep resistance is typically achieved when the γ′ phase constitutes 60–70% of the alloy []. Excessive γ′ particles would have a negative effect on the creep properties due to particle coarsening and embrittlement.
